title: God Who Cares
note:
Primary, Chapter 1, from the Mar Thoma Sunday School Samajam Primary Vol-1, pages 9–11. The flight into Egypt, told as a chapter about God seeing trouble before it arrives.

Memory verse and five-stage practice from the Memory Verse agent; see the verse note.

Games from the Game Builder agent (`npm run agent:games -- --class primary --chapter 01`). Its first run could not read two of the three questions: “To which place…” reached the generic “which” rule and came out `unsure` although the word “place” is in it, and “When did…” had no rule at all. Both went to multiple-choice by default, which is the outcome that agent exists to prevent. The classifier now reads places before sets and has a `time` category; the second run planned reveal, multiple-choice and sequence, which is what ships.

The fourth game is written by hand: three questions is below the Primary band’s four to five, and what it covers is the closing paragraph the question set skips.

Artwork downloaded from Drive (Primary / Chapter 01 / 04 - Story Artwork) and read panel by panel before a word of alt text was written; PNG to WebP at native size, no resize and no crop. Thirteen files — both covers and panels 1 to 11, contiguous, no duplicates, and every one of them exactly 941×1672 or its transpose. The first folder in this library to import with no warning of any kind.

The artwork brought a frame the text draft did not have; see the story note. Every game names a shelf picture, and “When They Went Home” is played on the chapter’s own panels rather than on text cards.

cover.note: Chapter 1’s own cover, drawn twice. The portrait has Joseph leading the donkey with Mary and the baby along a sunlit road, the Nile and the pyramids behind them, and “1” and “GOD WHO CARES” painted onto a label across the top — so the story reader lays no text over it. The landscape is the same journey at night and with no lettering: Herod scowls down from his balcony at the left with soldiers behind him, the family crosses the foreground, and the pyramids and one bright star stand at the right. Same chapter, same hand, and the one the chapter hub and the shelf row need since both draw their own heading.

story.alt: Night in a child’s bedroom. A boy sits up in bed clutching a dark blue blanket patterned with gold stars, a teddy and books on the shelf behind him and a full moon at the window. Halo glows beside him. The boy says, “Halo… I had a nightmare. I’m scared.” Halo answers, “Oh no… That sounds scary!”
story.note:
The chapter does not open in Bethlehem. The artwork frames the lesson with a boy waking from a nightmare in his own bed — panels 1 to 3 — crosses into the story at panel 4 with the boy still in the picture, tells the flight to Egypt and the return through panel 9, and comes back to the same bedroom in panels 10 and 11, in morning light, where the lesson lands as something the child can do. That frame is the artwork’s, and this is the fourth chapter in this library to turn out to have one.

The narration and the speech are lettered into the art, so no card carries `text` and every alt quotes the words painted on its own panel. “Amma” and “Appa” are the artwork’s own words and are left as they are.

Eleven panels where the text draft had sixteen cards. The draft is gone rather than reconciled, which is what happened to Beginner Chapters 5 and 6 and to Primary Chapter 3 as well.

story.alt: The same room. The boy has both hands on the blanket and is looking up. He says, “I wish Amma was here.” Halo, floating level with him, says, “Amma and Appa care for you very much.”
The boy has brightened, a hand at his chin. He says, “Amma and Appa care for me. Who else cares for me?” and then, “How do I know?” Halo answers, “God does. He cares for you wherever you are.”

The stable at Bethlehem, warm with lamplight. Mary sits on the straw with the swaddled baby in her arms and Joseph kneels beside her; a donkey looks over the rail and a lamb lies in the foreground, the town and one bright star beyond. The boy is in the scene now, in his pyjamas, watching. He asks, “Who are they?” and Halo says, “This is Mary, Joseph and baby Jesus.” The caption reads, “Long ago, Joseph, Mary and baby Jesus lived in Bethlehem.”

King Herod on his throne in a red and gold hall, a crown on his head and a scroll in one hand, jabbing a finger at a man who stands before him with his head bowed. Soldiers with spears line the wall under a banner with a gold lion on it. Herod says, “Find the child!” The caption reads, “King Herod heard that Jesus had been born. He was afraid that Jesus would become King and take his throne.”

Joseph asleep on a low bed, propped on one elbow and looking up, wide awake now. An angel in white leans towards him out of a warm light with one hand open; Mary and the baby sleep on behind. The angel says, “Get up! Take Jesus and Mary and go to Egypt,” and Joseph answers, “I will obey God.” The caption reads, “God knew that Jesus was in danger. So He sent an angel to warn Joseph.”

Out on the road at night. Joseph walks ahead with a bag over his shoulder, leading the donkey by its rein; Mary rides with the baby held close. Palms, a lit doorway and the moon behind them. Joseph says, “Come, Mary. We must leave now,” and Mary answers, “Yes, Joseph. Let’s go.” The caption reads, “Joseph obeyed God. That very night, he took Mary and baby Jesus and left for Egypt.”

The angel a second time, in the same warm light over Joseph’s bed, Mary and the child asleep behind. The angel says, “Get up! Take Jesus and Mary and go back,” and Joseph answers again, “I will obey God.” The caption reads, “After King Herod died, God sent an angel to Joseph again.”

Daylight, and the road home. Joseph walks with his staff and his bag, leading the donkey; Mary rides with the child, who is old enough now to look out at the road. A wooden signpost reads “Nazareth” and the hill town rises behind it among olive trees and flowers. The caption reads, “Joseph, Mary and Jesus returned from Egypt. They went to Nazareth and lived there. God cared for them every step of the way.”

Morning in the bedroom, the curtains open and sunlight on the quilt. The boy sits up smiling with Halo beside him; a hand-made poster on the wall reads “GOD IS WITH ME” under a red heart. The boy asks, “So God cared for Jesus and His family?” and Halo answers, “Yes. And God cares for you too.” The caption reads, “God knows when we are afraid. He cares for us.”

The boy sits on the edge of his bed in star-patterned pyjamas, holding a Holy Bible against his chest with both arms, a rocket and a stack of books on the bedside table. He says, “When I am scared, I can trust God!” and Halo answers, “Yes! God cares for you, and you can obey Him.” The caption reads, “God cares for me. I will trust and obey Him.”

curriculum.source: Primary Mar Thoma Vol-1, Chapter 01 “GOD WHO CARES”, p.10 — “ANSWER THE QUESTIONS”
curriculum.note:
The three questions the Primary book prints under the lesson on p.10, transcribed from the curriculum photographs in 01 - Curriculum Source.

The page carries the teacher’s own answer key in pen: ① brackets “King Herod was afraid that Jesus, who was born to be the King of the Jews, would take away his throne. So he sent his people to find and kill baby Jesus.”, the word “Egypt” is written beside question 2, and ③ brackets “After the death of king Herod, an angel appeared before Joseph and told him to return to Nazareth. So Joseph, Mary and baby Jesus went to Nazareth.” Each `answer` below is the sentence that mark points at, quoted from p.10 rather than reasoned out.

Three questions is below the Primary band’s four to five games, so a fourth was written by hand for the lesson’s closing paragraph — which the question set does not ask about at all, and which is the whole reason the chapter is called God Who Cares.

questions.question: Why did king Herod want to kill baby Jesus?
questions.objective: Herod was afraid that Jesus, born to be King of the Jews, would take away his throne.
questions.answer: “King Herod was afraid that Jesus, who was born to be the King of the Jews, would take away his throne. So he sent his people to find and kill baby Jesus.” (p.10)

questions.question: To which place did the angel tell Joseph to go?
questions.objective: Egypt — and that they went that same night, in complete obedience to God.
questions.answer: Egypt. “The angel told him to flee to Egypt with Mary and baby Jesus. In complete obedience to God, they fled to Egypt that night itself.” (p.10)
questions.note: The teacher has written “Egypt” beside this question in pen.

questions.question: When did the family of Jesus come back to Nazareth?
questions.objective: After king Herod died, when an angel appeared to Joseph a second time and told him to return.
questions.answer: “After the death of king Herod, an angel appeared before Joseph and told him to return to Nazareth. So Joseph, Mary and baby Jesus went to Nazareth.” (p.10)

games.title: Why Herod Was Afraid
games.objective: Follow the chain the lesson gives: Jesus was born King of the Jews, Herod feared for his throne, and so he sent his men.
games.note:
Question 1. A reveal rather than a quiz, because the lesson’s answer is not one fact but a chain of four, and a question with one right box would make a child choose between links that all belong. Nothing here is correct or incorrect; the four cards are the four steps in the order the page gives them.

Shelf picture: panel 5, Herod on his throne pointing and saying “Find the child!” — this game’s question drawn. The cards stay words: the panel’s own caption gives the whole answer, so putting it on a card would end the game before it began.

interactions.prompt: Turn over what the lesson says about Herod.

items.label: He sent men to kill Him

games.title: Where the Angel Sent Them
games.objective: Name Egypt — the place the angel told Joseph to flee to, and not one of the other three the chapter names.
games.note:
Question 2. Every wrong option is a real place in this same chapter — Bethlehem is where they were living, Nazareth is where they went afterwards, Jerusalem is Herod’s city — so the question is which one the angel named, not which one sounds like a place. That is the discrimination Primary is for; a Beginner’s version would put somewhere from a different story in the list. Four options is the band’s ceiling.

Shelf picture: panel 7, the family on the road at night. Panel 6 is the obvious choice and the wrong one — the angel’s speech bubble in it says “go to Egypt”, which is the answer printed on the shelf card. Panel 7 shows the leaving without naming where. The options stay words for the same reason.

interactions.prompt: Where did the angel tell Joseph to go?
interactions.hint: They went that same night, in complete obedience.

games.title: When They Went Home
games.objective: Put the escape and the return in order, so that "after Herod died" is something the child has placed rather than recited.
games.note:
Question 3 asks *when*, and when is a position rather than a fact — the lesson’s answer is “after the death of king Herod”, which only means anything next to what came before it. So the child puts five moments in order and the answer falls out of the ordering. Five steps, because the Primary band’s note says a sequence may run longer than four here.

This is the game the artwork changed. It was five text cards, and every step is now one of the chapter’s own panels in the order the artwork tells it — Herod on his throne, the first angel, the night road, the second angel, the signpost to Nazareth. Ordering pictures is what this mechanic wanted all along. The labels stay as captions so a child who reads gets both.

“King Herod died” was a step of its own in the text version and is not one here, because nothing in the artwork draws it — panel 8 reports it in its caption. The fact has moved into the hint, which is where the assistance ladder puts what a child needs rather than what they must already know.

Shelf picture: panel 8, the second angel — the moment question 3 is actually about, and not a picture either of the other games uses.

Worth knowing before a Sunday: panels 6 and 8 are nearly the same picture. The artist drew both angel visits identically — same angel, same room, Joseph giving the same answer — so shuffled side by side they cannot be told apart by looking. The captions are what separate them, which makes this a reading task as much as an ordering one. That suits Primary, where the band asks for understanding rather than recognition, and it would not suit Beginner at all.

interactions.hint: The second angel came after Herod died.

games.title: God Who Cares
games.objective: Hold the lesson's closing paragraph — God foresees our troubles, He helps us overcome them, and we must obey Him.
games.note:
The fourth game, written by hand because the book asks three questions and the Primary band wants four to five. What it covers is the paragraph the questions skip — the one the chapter is named after, and the only part of the page that is about the child rather than about Herod. Every false statement carries its reason immediately after it, and each reason is the lesson’s own sentence.

Shelf picture: panel 10, the boy back in his own bed in the morning under “God cares for you too” — which is this game’s subject, and the only panel that is about the child rather than about Herod.

interactions.prompt: Say what you think. Then we will look.

statements.source: God had foreseen the plan of king Herod.
statements.because: Yes. God had foreseen the plan of king Herod to kill Jesus, so He sent an angel to Joseph.
statements.note: Written back to front at first, and reported by the teacher. The statement was the false claim “God did not know what Herod was planning”, which made `answer` false — but the question asked the opposite way round, so a child answering “Did God know Herod’s plan?” was told No and then given a reason saying God had foreseen it. `source` never reaches the browser, so nothing but reading the two sentences together would show it. The statement now says what the lesson says, and the answer is yes.

statements.source: Joseph waited until morning before leaving.
statements.because: No. In complete obedience to God, they fled to Egypt that night itself.

statements.source: God foresees our troubles in life.
statements.ask: Does God see our troubles coming?
statements.because: Yes. The lesson says God foresees our troubles in life.

statements.source: God cares for us and helps us overcome our troubles.
statements.ask: Does God help us through them?
statements.because: Yes. As God cares for us, He will help us overcome them — and we must obey Him.

celebration.message: God saw the trouble coming, and He kept them safe.
celebration.note: The lesson’s closing thought, said back to the child.

verse.text: The Lord will keep you from all harm, He will watch over your life.

practice.hint: It begins with who keeps you.
words: He will watch over your life.
practice.note: Stage 1, phrase ordering — the Memory Verse agent’s Primary rung, used exactly as it came out. It cut the verse at its own comma, which is where it breathes.

practice.prompt: The Lord will keep you from all ______,
practice.note: Stage 2, the missing word with the clause whole around it. Four options where a Beginner gets three, and every one a real word of this verse.

practice.prompt: The Lord will keep you from all harm, He will ______
practice.hint: What does a shepherd do from the hillside?
practice.note: Stage 3, the same question with the right-hand side taken away. “keep” reads perfectly well in that gap and is the verse’s own earlier verb, so the only thing separating them is remembering the sentence forwards.
Stage 4, full reconstruction — six pieces where stage 1 had three, which is the whole of the difference between the two stages.

practice.prompt: Where does our verse come from?
practice.hint: It is one of the Psalms.
practice.note: Stage 5, the reference — recognised, not typed; the Primary band does not write references yet. St. Matthew 2 is this chapter’s own Bible Portion, printed on p.9, and Psalms 21 is the same number with a digit missing.

verse.note:
Read from the chapter’s last page through the Memory Verse agent: `--fetch --source-dir` over the curriculum photographs, the supervised read, then `--from-extraction`. That page lives in `06 - Memory Verse` rather than in `01 - Curriculum Source`, which is why this chapter first shipped without a verse at all — the agent was pointed at the wrong folder, not at a gap.

Five stages in the shape Primary Chapter 3 uses: phrase ordering, a gap with the sentence whole on both sides of it, the same gap with the right-hand side taken away, a finer reconstruction, and the reference chosen against near misses. Translation is unresolved: the page does not name one, which is where every chapter in this library stands.

Printed as “Psalms 121: 7” — plural, with a space after the colon — and both are kept as printed.

Picture: panel 9, the road to Nazareth under the words “God cared for them every step of the way” — which is this verse in the chapter’s own sentence.

decision.statement: God cares for me. I will obey his words.
decision.note: The curriculum’s own My Decision line from p.12, unchanged, including its lower-case “his”.

song.note: The Song from p.12, in the Latin script the book prints it in, line for line.

prayer.text: Caring Lord, help me to obey Your will in my life. Amen
prayer.note: The closing Prayer from p.12, word for word including its Amen with no full stop. The chapter also opens with a prayer on p.9 — “Thank you Lord, for caring for us always. Bless us that we may live in obedience to You. Amen.” — which has nowhere to go in this shape and is recorded here rather than lost.
